clue.text: Mystical scientist sending river into European country marsh

parts.note: a Scandinavian country

indicators.note: to send one thing into another is to push it inside, so a piece goes within a word

parts.note: a bog is wet marshy ground
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A mystic scientist diverts a river into a marshy foreign land.
explanation.walkthrough: The river goes into the marsh only, not the country. Emanuel Swedenborg was an 18th-century Swedish scientist who turned to mystical theology.
explanation.definitionFit: Swedenborg began as a working engineer and naturalist before his visionary religious writings, so he fits both halves of the description.

clue.text: I note failure to restrain large pet

definitions.note: an adjective here, as in a pet project: favoured, spoilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone admits failing to keep a big pet animal under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like an animal noun but is the definition in its adjective sense. 'Large' is abbreviated to three letters here, not the usual single L.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet child or pet theory is one that is favoured and spoilt, exactly what an indulged one is.

clue.text: Seed a Parisian turned up in vegetable matter

explanation.walkthrough: 'A Parisian' means the French word for 'a', not a person from Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: The peanut is botanically the edible seed of a legume pod, despite the nut in its common name.

clue.text: A lot of commotion about dull inspiration

parts.note: taken as written
a fuss is a commotion
flat means dull or lifeless

explanation.surface: Lots of excitement surrounds a rather dreary source of creativity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' looks like one phrase meaning much, but the A stands alone and 'lot of' only trims the commotion word.
explanation.definitionFit: Afflatus is a literary word for a sudden creative or divine impulse, the breath of the muse.

clue.text: Ionised gas: contrived a sample to emit energy

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lab report: a gas sample is rigged so that it gives off energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one E from A SAMPLE and rearrange the remaining six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicists call a gas so hot that its atoms are stripped of electrons the fourth state of matter, plasma.

clue.text: Strange Buddhist priest heading heavenwards, newly born inside

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd Buddhist priest ascends to heaven carrying a newborn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newly born' reads as a newborn baby, but 'newly' rearranges the letters of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something that departs from what is usual or expected, making them simple synonyms.

clue.text: Doctor satisfied about national importance

explanation.surface: A doctor is pleased about something of national significance.

explanation.definitionFit: In formal English a matter of great moment is one of great significance or weight.

clue.text: Question importing English dairy product

explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside WHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Whey is the watery liquid left after milk curdles in cheesemaking, a by-product of the dairy.

clue.text: Splendid Welsh league accepting representation of founder

taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh league' reads as one body, but it splits into W and L, which hold a rearranged FOUNDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are everyday terms of high praise for something excellent or marvellous.

clue.text: Relative turned about to go for soup

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative turned' looks like a reversal of the relative, but it is RE that turns to ER, and that ER is dropped from the end of BROTHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Broth is a thin soup of meat or vegetables simmered in stock.

clue.text: Face consuming supply of tea every 24 hours

explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' is not a human face but the face of a clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Diurnal describes something recurring daily, on a cycle of one day.

clue.text: Former Queen in flamboyant clothing, experiencing damp weather

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: showy means flashy or flamboyant

explanation.surface: The late monarch, dressed extravagantly, is caught in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former' fits because Elizabeth II, whose cipher was Elizabeth Regina, is no longer the reigning monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Showery weather brings frequent brief spells of rain, so a showery day is one with damp conditions.

clue.text: Dark period with good hearts suppressed by idiot

indicators.note: to be suppressed is to be held down and kept in, so pieces sit within another word

parts.note: a nit, or nitwit, is a fool

explanation.walkthrough: G and H sit inside NIT. 'Good hearts' reads as kind people, but each word is just one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the time between sunset and sunrise when it is dark.

clue.text: Try dropping unknown firearm, not given to wounding

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something not given is withheld, so those letters are left out

parts.note: an automatic is a self-loading gun
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not given to wounding' reads as a pacifist; in fact 'not given' strips the word 'to' from AUTOMATIC, and 'wounding' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Traumatic comes from the Greek for wound, and describes injuries to body or mind.

clue.text: Storyteller has buckled horn carried by vagrant cleric

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A storyteller owns a bent horn carried by a wandering priest.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two separate anagrams here, and the first sits inside the second just after its opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicler records events in narrative form, so is a teller of history's stories.

clue.text: Such characters in old ode?

definitions.note: refers back to the kind of characters described: the answer word fills the gap 'such characters'

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters of the two words run together

explanation.surface: Are there strange figures in an ancient poem?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes itself: the answer is the kind of characters taken, the odd-numbered ones, and those letters spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd letters are those at positions one, three, five, and the same word means peculiar, so 'such' points back to it.

clue.text: Feel pride, say, after former schoolfellow returned as biographer

parts.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil
to swell with pride; 'say' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: An old classmate comes back as a life-writer, and you feel proud.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy is a former pupil of a British school. James Boswell wrote the celebrated Life of Samuel Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: Boswell's Life of Johnson made his name a byword for a devoted biographer.

clue.text: Spooner's to miss party, leading to unpleasant response

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial consonants trade places

parts.note: to lack something is to miss it
a bash is a party
the two words spoken with their opening consonants swapped

explanation.surface: Skipping a party causes a hostile reaction.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of LACK BASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlash is a strong adverse reaction against some development or decision.

clue.text: Cut up about greeting piece of early evidence?

indicators.note: about means around, so one thing surrounds another

a casual hello
a bit is a piece

explanation.surface: A cut-up fragment is presented as the first proof in a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of' looks like a link into the definition, but it is wordplay in its own right; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In a courtroom the first item of evidence put before the jury is labelled with the opening letter of the alphabet.

clue.text: Title is backed by publisher finally

indicators.note: by means next to, so the pieces are set side by side

parts.note: taken as written

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed by' reads as supported by; here 'backed' reverses the word and 'by' simply places R next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir is the honorific used by knights and baronets, a formal title of rank.

clue.text: Malaysian dish keeping Pakistani all but enthralled for 24 hours

parts.note: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan

explanation.surface: A Malaysian meal keeps a Pakistani diner captivated for a whole day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pakistani' is not a person but the country's national language.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturday is one day of the week, and any single day lasts a full 24 hours.

clue.text: Number of attendees to drop? Get in without paying

explanation.surface: Falling crowd numbers, so sneak in for free.
explanation.walkthrough: A gate in British sport is the number of spectators at a match. The question mark splits the clue in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To gatecrash is to enter an event uninvited or without a ticket.

clue.text: Bird in quantity of film after holiday cut short

clue.text: Rough area, dry, containing phosphorus

clue.text: Horseplay when coming round to bed

taken as written

clue.text: Time in Church House, ignoring special sponsorship
